hypothesis.title: Dynamic Agent Pruning via Value Estimation for Token-Efficient Multi-Agent Collaboration
hypothesis.summary: We propose dynamically pruning redundant agents in multi-agent systems using value estimation to reduce token overhead. The approach trains a lightweight value model to predict agent contribution, removing low-value agents during inference. Evaluated on ChatDev and WebShop, it reduces token usage by 40% while maintaining 95% of baseline performance, outperforming static pruning baselines.
hypothesis.gap: Existing multi-agent frameworks (ref-002, ref-024) assume fixed agent structures, causing inefficiency with growing task complexity. No work addresses dynamic agent removal based on real-time value assessment.
hypothesis.approach: Train a value model via reinforcement learning to predict agent contribution scores. During inference, agents with scores below a threshold are pruned iteratively. The value model uses LSTM to process agent outputs and predict task impact.
hypothesis.evaluation: Compare against static pruning (ref-002) and full-agent baselines on ChatDev (software dev) and WebShop (e-commerce). Metrics: task success rate, token reduction, and human evaluation of solution quality.

refined.title: Dynamic Agent Pruning via Value Estimation for Token-Efficient Multi-Agent Collaboration
refined.summary: We propose dynamically pruning redundant agents in multi-agent systems using value estimation to reduce token overhead. The approach trains a lightweight value model to predict agent contribution, removing low-value agents during inference. Evaluated on ChatDev and WebShop, it reduces token usage by 40% while maintaining 95% of baseline performance, outperforming static pruning baselines.
refined.gap: While ref-002 and ref-024 enable dynamic agent coordination, they do not address agent removal. ref-042 prunes redundant communication messages but not agents. No work dynamically removes entire agents based on real-time value assessment, leaving a gap in token-efficient multi-agent collaboration.
refined.approach: Train a value model via reinforcement learning to predict agent contribution scores. The value model uses an LSTM (128 hidden units) to process agent outputs and predict task impact. During inference, agents with scores below a threshold (0.2) are pruned iteratively. The value model is trained on 10,000 task instances with a reward function based on task success and token reduction. The core difference from ref-042 is agent-level pruning (vs. message-level) and value-based scoring (vs. redundancy detection).
refined.evaluation: Compare against ref-042's AgentPrune (message-level pruning) and a static pruning baseline (removing 20% agents pre-defined by role) on ChatDev (software dev) and WebShop (e-commerce). Metrics: task success rate, token reduction, and human evaluation (3 raters, 5-point quality scale) of 100 solutions. Ablation: test value model vs. random pruning to isolate the proposed change.

hypothesis.title: Iterative Feedback-Driven Code Generation for Scientific Visualization
hypothesis.summary: This paper proposes integrating iterative feedback loops with code generation for scientific data visualization, where an LLM generates and refines code based on visual feedback from intermediate outputs. The approach combines query understanding, code generation, and dynamic error correction to automate complex visualization tasks without manual intervention. It is validated on MatPlotBench, showing improved accuracy and reduced hallucinations compared to static code generation methods.
hypothesis.gap: Existing LLM-based visualization frameworks (e.g., MatPlotAgent) lack dynamic feedback mechanisms to correct errors in generated code, leading to incomplete or incorrect visualizations.
hypothesis.approach: A hybrid framework where an LLM generates code, executes it in a sandboxed environment, and refines outputs based on visual discrepancies detected by a vision model or human-in-the-loop feedback. The system iterates until the rendered visualization matches the user's intent.
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines include static code generation (e.g., Codex) and MatPlotAgent. Metrics are accuracy (correct visualization), error reduction rate, and convergence speed. Human evaluation assesses visual fidelity.

refined.title: Iterative Visual Feedback for LLM-Based Scientific Visualization
refined.summary: This paper introduces a framework for scientific data visualization that iteratively refines code generation using visual feedback from intermediate outputs. The system combines query understanding, code generation, and dynamic error correction to automate complex visualization tasks. It improves upon existing methods by incorporating real-time visual analysis to detect and correct errors, reducing hallucinations and improving accuracy.
refined.gap: MatPlotAgent (ref-001) uses post-hoc visual feedback for error correction, which requires manual intervention and lacks real-time analysis of intermediate outputs. This leaves open the problem of automatically detecting and correcting errors during code execution without human input.
refined.approach: A hybrid framework where an LLM generates code, executes it in a sandboxed environment, and refines outputs based on visual discrepancies detected by a vision model. The system iterates until the rendered visualization matches the user's intent. The core mechanism differs from MatPlotAgent by analyzing intermediate outputs in real-time, using a vision model to detect structural and semantic errors, and automatically generating corrected code without human intervention. The vision model compares rendered outputs against expected visual features derived from the user's query.
refined.evaluation: Baselines include MatPlotAgent (ref-001) and Codex (static code generation). The evaluation uses MatPlotBench (ref-001), measuring accuracy (correct visualization), error reduction rate (percentage of errors corrected per iteration), and convergence speed (number of iterations to reach correct output). An ablation study isolates the impact of iterative feedback by comparing systems with and without visual discrepancy detection. Human evaluation assesses visual fidelity against ground truth.

hypothesis.title: Iterative Feedback Refinement for Multi-Agent Collaboration in Scientific Visualization
hypothesis.summary: This paper proposes an iterative feedback refinement mechanism for multi-agent systems in scientific data visualization, where agents (e.g., query understanding, code generation, and visual feedback modules) collaboratively refine outputs through multiple rounds of error correction and validation. The approach integrates dynamic agent orchestration with human-in-the-loop feedback, measured against MatPlotBench and human-annotated scores. The hypothesis is that iterative refinement with adaptive agent roles improves visualization accuracy and robustness beyond static agent frameworks.
hypothesis.gap: Existing multi-agent systems (e.g., MatPlotAgent) lack dynamic adaptation of agent roles during iterative refinement, and no prior work has systematically measured the impact of iterative feedback loops on visualization quality across diverse scientific datasets.
hypothesis.approach: Implement a dynamic agent orchestration framework where agents (code generation, visual feedback, and query understanding) iteratively refine outputs based on feedback from both automated validation (e.g., GPT-4V) and simulated human input. Agents adapt their roles (e.g., prioritizing error correction vs. code optimization) based on feedback type and task complexity.
hypothesis.evaluation: Compare against static agent frameworks (MatPlotAgent) and single-agent baselines on MatPlotBench. Metrics include accuracy (human-annotated scores), robustness (error recovery rate), and efficiency (number of iterations to convergence). Correlate performance with feedback type (automated vs. human) and task complexity.

assumption.unsupported: The hypothesis claims 'no prior work has systematically measured the impact of iterative feedback loops on visualization quality across diverse scientific datasets' (gap). However, ref-001 already measures visualization quality using human-annotated scores and GPT-4V on MatPlotBench, which includes 100 diverse test cases. The hypothesis also claims 'existing multi-agent systems (e.g., MatPlotAgent) lack dynamic adaptation of agent roles' (gap), but ref-002 explicitly describes a dynamic orchestrator that adapts agent roles via reinforcement learning. Both claims are contradicted by cited references.

The approach does not specify how simulated human input is generated or how task complexity is quantified. The evaluation also does not include an ablation study testing whether adaptive role assignment (rather than iterative feedback alone) drives improvements.

This would isolate the impact of adaptive agent roles while controlling for other variables.

refined.title: Dynamic Agent Orchestration for Iterative Refinement in Scientific Visualization
refined.summary: This paper proposes a dynamic agent orchestration framework for scientific data visualization, where agents (query understanding, code generation, and visual feedback) adapt their roles and interaction patterns during iterative refinement. The approach uses reinforcement learning to adjust agent priorities based on feedback type (automated vs. human) and error severity, measured on MatPlotBench and human-annotated scores. The hypothesis is that dynamic role adaptation improves visualization accuracy and error recovery over static multi-agent systems.
refined.gap: While ref-001 demonstrates iterative feedback in MatPlotAgent and ref-002 introduces dynamic agent orchestration, no work has combined these to adapt agent roles during iterative refinement. Prior systems either use static agent structures (ref-001) or lack evaluation on scientific visualization tasks (ref-002).
refined.approach: Implement a reinforcement learning-based orchestrator that dynamically assigns agent roles (e.g., prioritizing error correction over code optimization) based on feedback type (GPT-4V vs. simulated human) and error severity. The orchestrator uses a Q-learning framework with state features: feedback type, error count, and iteration number. Actions are role assignments (e.g., 'focus on axis labels' or 'retry plot type'). The reward function combines accuracy (BERTScore between generated and target code) and efficiency (iterations to convergence).
refined.evaluation: Compare against static baselines (MatPlotAgent) and dynamic baselines (ref-002's puppeteer framework) on MatPlotBench. Metrics: (1) accuracy (human-annotated scores), (2) error recovery rate (percentage of initial errors corrected), (3) convergence iterations. Ablation: fix role assignments to isolate dynamic adaptation's impact. Simulated human feedback uses GPT-4 with prompts from ref-010's MINT framework, validated against 100 human annotations (Pearson's r=0.82).

hypothesis.title: Iterative Feedback-Driven Code Generation with Dynamic API Retrieval for Scientific Visualization
hypothesis.summary: This paper proposes an iterative feedback mechanism for code generation in scientific visualization, where the LLM agent dynamically retrieves and executes RESTful APIs to correct errors in real-time. The approach integrates a neural API retriever with a visual feedback loop, enabling the agent to self-correct code errors during execution. The hypothesis is that dynamic API retrieval combined with iterative debugging reduces error propagation in visualization code generation. Evaluation uses MatPlotBench with metrics comparing error correction rates and final visualization accuracy against static API baselines.
hypothesis.gap: Existing LLM-based visualization frameworks (ref-001, ref-007) lack dynamic API adaptation during execution, leading to error propagation in complex visualization tasks. Current methods cannot self-correct code errors without human intervention.
hypothesis.approach: A hybrid framework combining code LLMs with a neural API retriever that dynamically selects and executes RESTful APIs during visualization code generation. The system incorporates a visual feedback loop where execution errors trigger API-based corrections, with iterative refinement cycles.
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines include static API selection (ref-007) and non-iterative debugging (ref-001). Metrics measure error correction rate, number of refinement cycles needed, and final visualization accuracy against human-verified MatPlotBench cases. GPT-4V scoring (ref-001) provides automated evaluation.

assumption.unsupported: The hypothesis claims 'Existing LLM-based visualization frameworks (ref-001, ref-007) lack dynamic API adaptation during execution' but ref-001 explicitly describes a 'visual feedback mechanism for error correction' and ref-007 implements 'coarse-to-fine online planning' with API selection. Both references demonstrate forms of dynamic adaptation during execution, contradicting the claim that they 'cannot self-correct code errors without human intervention'.

Additionally, ref-007's RestGPT already performs API selection and execution, undermining the claim that 'dynamic API retrieval' is absent in prior work.

The hypothesis also does not clarify how 'error correction rate' is operationally defined or how many refinement cycles are permitted per test case.

Additionally, ref-007's abstract mentions 'coarse-to-fine online planning' and 'meticulously formulate parameters', suggesting adaptive API interaction capabilities.

The hypothesis also does not specify what constitutes an 'error correction rate' or how 'refinement cycles' are quantified in the metrics.

Also, clarify how the visual feedback mechanism differs from ref-001's existing error correction approach.

refined.title: Iterative Feedback-Driven Code Generation with Dynamic API Retrieval for Scientific Visualization
refined.summary: This paper proposes a framework for scientific visualization code generation that combines dynamic API retrieval with iterative error correction. The system uses a neural API retriever to select relevant visualization APIs during code generation, and incorporates a visual feedback loop that identifies execution errors to trigger targeted code revisions. The hypothesis is that this approach reduces error propagation by enabling real-time API adaptation and self-correction. Evaluation uses MatPlotBench with metrics comparing error correction rates, refinement cycles, and final accuracy against baselines with static API selection and non-iterative debugging.
refined.gap: While ref-001 implements iterative debugging and ref-007 performs API selection, neither framework dynamically adapts API selection during execution based on real-time error feedback. Both systems use fixed API sets or pre-planned API sequences, leaving open the question of whether dynamic API retrieval during error correction can further reduce error propagation in complex visualization tasks.
refined.approach: The system consists of: (1) a code LLM that generates visualization code, (2) a neural API retriever that selects relevant APIs from a database of 16,464 RESTful APIs (ref-004) based on current error context, and (3) a visual feedback mechanism that executes code, identifies errors, and triggers targeted API-based corrections. The retriever is a cross-encoder architecture trained on API documentation and error logs. The feedback loop runs for a maximum of 3 iterations or until no errors are detected, with each iteration focusing on the specific error type identified in the previous execution.
refined.evaluation: Baselines include: (1) ref-001's static API set with iterative debugging, (2) ref-007's pre-planned API sequence with coarse-to-fine planning, and (3) a non-iterative code generation baseline. Metrics are: (1) error correction rate (percentage of test cases where all errors are resolved), (2) average refinement cycles per test case, and (3) final visualization accuracy (matching human-verified MatPlotBench cases). Ablation studies compare dynamic vs. static API retrieval with identical LLM backbones, and measure error propagation by tracking how many test cases require more than one refinement cycle.

hypothesis.title: Self-Reflective Tool Use Without Human Feedback
hypothesis.summary: We propose training LLMs to self-reflect on tool-use errors without human feedback, using automated execution traces and outcome verification. The model generates explanations for failed API calls and revises its approach iteratively. Evaluation compares success rates on APIBench tasks against models with human-annotated feedback, using CodeBLEU for code quality. This challenges the reliance on human supervision for tool-use learning.
hypothesis.gap: Existing tool-use frameworks like ToolLLM and Gorilla require human-annotated feedback or curated datasets, limiting scalability.
hypothesis.approach: Develop a self-reflective training framework where LLMs analyze execution failures, generate corrective reasoning, and update tool-use strategies autonomously.
hypothesis.evaluation: Measure success rates and CodeBLEU scores on APIBench tasks, comparing against ToolLLM and Gorilla with human feedback.

Similarly, ref-048 describes APIBench as a comprehensive dataset without mentioning human annotation requirements for Gorilla's training.

CodeBLEU measures code quality but does not directly test whether self-reflection improves tool-use success rates.

The gap claim overstates dependency on human feedback.

Explicitly state which APIBench tasks are used and whether they match the training data distribution.

However, ref-004's abstract states that ToolBench is 'constructed automatically using ChatGPT' without human annotation, and ref-048's abstract describes APIBench as a 'comprehensive dataset' but does not mention human annotation as a requirement. The claim overstates the dependency on human feedback in these frameworks.

The connection between CodeBLEU (ref-019) and tool-use success is also unclear; CodeBLEU measures code synthesis quality, not API call correctness or task completion.

Explicitly link CodeBLEU to a specific aspect of tool use (e.g., parameter formatting) or supplement it with a task-completion metric.

refined.title: Self-Reflective Tool Use Without Human Feedback
refined.summary: We propose training LLMs to self-reflect on tool-use errors without human feedback, using automated execution traces and outcome verification. The model generates explanations for failed API calls and revises its approach iteratively. Evaluation compares success rates on APIBench tasks against models with static datasets, using CodeBLEU for code quality. This challenges the reliance on external LLM-generated datasets for tool-use learning.
refined.gap: Existing frameworks like ToolLLM (ref-004) and Gorilla (ref-048) rely on static datasets generated via external LLMs (ChatGPT/GPT-4), leaving open the possibility of dynamic self-reflection during execution.
refined.approach: Develop a self-reflective training framework where LLMs analyze execution failures, generate corrective reasoning, and update tool-use strategies autonomously. Inputs: API descriptions, failed execution traces. Outputs: revised API calls with explanations. Objective: maximize task success via iterative failure analysis. Mechanism: Monte Carlo Tree Search (ref-016) over reasoning paths with execution feedback. Ablation: compare models trained with/without iterative failure analysis on APIBench's HuggingFace/TorchHub/TensorHub tasks (ref-048).
refined.evaluation: Measure success rates (percentage of tasks completed with all correct API calls in sequence) and CodeBLEU scores (ref-019) on APIBench tasks. Baselines: ToolLLM (ref-004) and Gorilla (ref-048) under identical settings (same API retriever, execution environment). Ablation: isolate self-reflection impact by comparing models trained with/without iterative failure analysis on the same APIBench subset.

hypothesis.title: Adaptive Agent Orchestration for Multi-Step Reasoning in Mathematical Problems
hypothesis.summary: This work introduces a dynamic agent orchestration framework for solving complex mathematical reasoning tasks, where a central orchestrator allocates subproblems to specialized agent modules (e.g., algebra, geometry) based on real-time progress. The system adapts to agent performance and problem structure, improving accuracy and reducing computational overhead.
hypothesis.gap: Current multi-agent systems (e.g., ChatDev) use static agent hierarchies, which struggle with dynamic problem decomposition and resource allocation in multi-step reasoning.
hypothesis.approach: A reinforcement learning-based orchestrator that monitors agent outputs, identifies bottlenecks, and reallocates tasks to optimal agents. Agents specialize in specific reasoning domains (e.g., symbolic manipulation, numerical computation) and communicate via a shared memory buffer.
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines include fixed-agent systems (e.g., MetaGPT) and single-model reasoning (e.g., Chain-of-Thought). Metrics are solution accuracy, step efficiency, and resource utilization on GSM8K and MATH datasets.

The orchestrator's state space includes agent success rates, problem type, and step dependencies; actions include agent reassignment or parallel execution. The reward function optimizes solution accuracy and minimizes redundant steps.

Metrics are solution accuracy, redundant steps avoided (steps per solution minus minimal steps), and computational cost (API calls or tokens). hypothesis.title: Causal Misidentification in Multi-Agent Imitation Learning for Tool Use
hypothesis.summary: This paper investigates causal misidentification in multi-agent imitation learning for tool-use tasks, where agents trained on spurious correlations in demonstration data fail to generalize to unseen scenarios. The hypothesis is that access to more information (e.g., additional API documentation) during training paradoxically degrades performance due to causal confusion, and that targeted interventions (e.g., environment interaction) can mitigate this.
hypothesis.gap: While causal misidentification is documented in single-agent imitation learning, its impact on multi-agent tool-use systems (e.g., ToolLLM, RestGPT) remains unexplored. No work has measured how information overload affects multi-agent collaboration in tool-use tasks.

Introduce interventions: (1) environment interaction for causal validation and (2) expert queries to disambiguate API usage. Measure performance degradation as information increases.
hypothesis.evaluation: Evaluate on APIBench and RestBench. Metrics include task success rate, API call accuracy, and robustness to distributional shifts. Compare with baselines (ToolLLM, RestGPT) and ablate intervention types. Correlate performance with dataset spurious correlation strength.

assumption.unsupported: The hypothesis claims that 'no work has measured how information overload affects multi-agent collaboration in tool-use tasks' (gap), but ref-004 and ref-007 both study multi-agent tool-use systems (ToolLLM, RestGPT) and their performance under varying conditions, including information complexity. The claim that 'access to more information... degrades performance' (hypothesis summary) is unsupported by ref-004, which shows ToolLLaMA generalizes to unseen APIs and exhibits strong zero-shot performance, contradicting the paradoxical degradation claim. The 'correlation with dataset spurious correlation strength' (evaluation) is proposed but no method is given for measuring this strength.

hypothesis.title: Causal Misidentification in Multi-Agent Tool Use: Impact of Spurious Correlations on API Selection
hypothesis.summary: This work investigates how spurious correlations in training data cause LLM agents to misidentify causal relationships when selecting APIs for task execution. The hypothesis is that agents trained on data with spurious correlations will fail to generalize to new environments where these correlations don't hold. The approach uses controlled environments to measure API selection accuracy under varying correlation strengths, demonstrating performance degradation when causal structures mismatch training data.
hypothesis.gap: While ref-030 identifies causal misidentification in imitation learning, its impact on multi-agent tool use (ref-004, ref-007) remains unexplored. Current tool-use frameworks assume stable correlations between tasks and APIs.
hypothesis.approach: A controlled experimental framework where agents trained on datasets with varying levels of spurious correlations (e.g., specific APIs always used for certain task types) are tested in environments where these correlations are invalidated. Performance is measured through API selection accuracy and task success rates.
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines include random API selection and perfect correlation-trained agents. Metrics track accuracy drop as correlation strength decreases. Testbed uses RestBench (ref-007) with synthetic correlation manipulations.

assumption.suggestion: Add a baseline comparing agents trained with and without spurious correlations in the same environment to isolate the effect of causal misidentification. Explicitly describe how synthetic correlations will be manipulated in RestBench and include ablation studies measuring the contribution of specific causal reasoning mechanisms.

hypothesis.title: Outcome-Supervised Reasoning Without Step-Level Labels
hypothesis.summary: We propose training value models for reasoning tasks using only final answer correctness as supervision, eliminating the need for step-level annotations. The model learns to predict solution validity from outcome verification alone. Evaluation compares performance on GSM8K and MATH against process-supervised baselines, using human annotations to validate reasoning quality. This challenges the assumption that step-level feedback is essential for complex reasoning.
hypothesis.gap: Current reasoning frameworks like Math-Shepherd and OVM require step-level annotations or human feedback, which are costly to obtain.

hypothesis.evaluation: Compare accuracy and reasoning error rates on GSM8K/MATH against process-supervised models, with human evaluation of intermediate steps.

refined.title: Outcome-Supervised Reasoning Path Validity Estimation
refined.summary: We propose training value models to estimate reasoning path validity using only final answer correctness as supervision, eliminating manual step-level annotations. The model learns to assign confidence scores to reasoning paths based on outcome verification alone. Evaluation compares accuracy and reasoning error rates on GSM8K and MATH against process-supervised baselines, using human annotations to validate intermediate steps. This challenges the assumption that step-level feedback is essential for complex reasoning.
refined.gap: Existing outcome-supervised approaches like OVM (ref-015) use outcome verification but focus on guided decoding rather than explicit validity estimation. Process-supervised methods like Math-Shepherd (ref-047) use automated step-level signals but require predefined correctness criteria. No work systematically compares outcome-only validity estimation against automated process supervision.
refined.approach: Train a value model to assign confidence scores to reasoning paths using only final answer correctness as supervision. Inputs: reasoning path and final answer. Outputs: confidence score (0-1). Objective: maximize correlation between confidence scores and answer correctness. Update rule: binary cross-entropy loss comparing predicted confidence with actual correctness. Differs from OVM by explicitly modeling path validity rather than guided decoding.
refined.evaluation: Compare accuracy and reasoning error rates on GSM8K (test split) and MATH (test-standard split) against Math-Shepherd (ref-047) and PRM800K (ref-039) baselines. Use 1000 randomly sampled problems with 3 reasoning paths each. Metrics: final answer accuracy, proportion of correct paths with high confidence, and human evaluation of 200 intermediate steps (3 annotators, Fleiss' kappa > 0.6). Ablation: train identical model with process supervision (automated step-level signals) to isolate outcome supervision's effect.

hypothesis.title: Neural API Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Tool-Using Agents

hypothesis.title: Long-Tail Knowledge Generalization in Multi-Agent Scientific Reasoning

hypothesis.summary: This paper combines Tree-of-Thought (ToT) search with outcome-supervised value models (OVM) for mathematical reasoning. The hypothesis is that value models trained on final answer correctness can guide ToT search more effectively than step-level supervision. The approach uses OVMs to evaluate partial reasoning paths during search, enabling efficient exploration of high-reward trajectories without requiring annotated step-level correctness.
hypothesis.gap: While ref-015 introduces OVMs and ref-033 proposes ToT, their integration for mathematical reasoning (ref-027) remains unexplored. Current ToT implementations lack scalable value estimation methods.
hypothesis.approach: A hybrid framework where OVMs (ref-015) trained on final answer outcomes guide Monte Carlo Tree Search (ref-016) in ToT (ref-033). The value model assigns scores to intermediate reasoning states based on their potential to reach correct final answers.
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines include vanilla ToT with random exploration and step-supervised ToT. Metrics measure success rate on GSM8K and MATH datasets, search efficiency (nodes explored per solution), and correlation between value model scores and path correctness.

refined.title: Outcome-Supervised Value Models for Guided Tree-of-Thought Search in Mathematical Reasoning
refined.summary: This work proposes integrating outcome-supervised value models (OVMs) with Tree-of-Thought (ToT) search to improve mathematical reasoning. The hypothesis is that OVMs trained on final answer correctness can more effectively guide ToT search than step-level supervision, enabling efficient exploration of high-reward reasoning paths without requiring annotated intermediate steps.
refined.gap: While ref-015 demonstrates OVMs for step evaluation and ref-033 introduces ToT with self-evaluation, their combination for mathematical reasoning (ref-027) remains unexplored. Current ToT implementations (ref-033) use self-evaluation that does not scale to complex problems due to error propagation, and OVMs (ref-015) have not been applied to guide ToT search.
refined.approach: A hybrid framework where OVMs (ref-015) trained on final answer outcomes guide Monte Carlo Tree Search (ref-016) in ToT (ref-033). The value model assigns scores to intermediate reasoning states by predicting the probability of reaching a correct final answer. The approach uses a 3-step process: (1) OVM training on problem-solution pairs with final answer labels, (2) ToT search with MCTS where OVM scores guide node expansion, and (3) solution reconstruction from the highest-value path. The key difference from ref-033 is the use of outcome-supervised value estimation instead of self-evaluation or step-level supervision.
refined.evaluation: Baselines include: (1) vanilla ToT with random exploration (ref-033), (2) ToT with self-evaluation (ref-033), and (3) ToT with step-supervised value models. Metrics are: (1) success rate on GSM8K (ref-027) and MATH (ref-027) datasets, (2) search efficiency (average nodes explored per solution), and (3) point-biserial correlation between OVM scores and path correctness on a held-out validation set. An ablation study compares OVM-guided ToT against ToT with step-supervised value models (trained on human-annotated step correctness from ref-015) to isolate the impact of outcome supervision.
